subtitle: Recognize prohibited and restrictive practices, follow Minnesota's emergency manual restraint and reporting requirements, and steer plans toward person-centered positive supports that improve quality of life.
audience: For case managers and care coordinators, lead agency staff, 245D provider oversight and licensing-adjacent staff, and DSD program, policy and supervisory staff who review support plans, incident reports or provider practices for people with disabilities.

lessons.title: Why Minnesota moved to positive supports
objectives: Identify which providers and settings the Positive Supports Rule applies to.
Explain the four purposes for which 245D prohibits restrictive procedures.
Describe the quality-of-life goals DHS names for the rule.
Compare a compliance-only reading of the rule with a quality-of-life reading.
lessons.teaching:
Minnesota's Positive Supports Rule, Minnesota Rules chapter 9544, works together with Minnesota Statutes chapter 245D to govern how licensed providers respond to behavior that concerns them. The rule applies to providers of home and community-based services governed by chapter 245D, which serve people with disabilities and people sixty-five and older, and to other settings licensed under chapter 245A that serve people with a developmental disability or related condition. DHS describes the rule's purpose as improving the quality of life for people, including children, who receive DHS-licensed services, by requiring person-centered principles and positive support strategies.

The core prohibition sits in 245D. A license holder may not use chemical restraint, mechanical restraint, manual restraint, time out, seclusion, or any other aversive or deprivation procedure as a substitute for adequate staffing, as a behavioral or therapeutic program to reduce or eliminate behavior, as punishment, or for staff convenience. Those four purposes are worth memorizing, because they describe the reasons restrictive practices have historically crept into services. When you review a plan or a report, ask whether a restriction is really serving one of those purposes, even if no one would say so out loud.

DHS lists the goals behind the rule: community participation and inclusion in the most integrated setting, high-quality environments, positive support strategies developed together with the person, growth in skills and self-determination, better quality of life, freedom from humiliating and demeaning procedures, and an end to aversive and deprivation procedures, with consistent standards across settings. Notice that most of these are about what should be present in a person's life, not only what should be absent.

That difference shapes oversight. A compliance-only reading asks whether prohibited procedures were avoided and reports were filed on time. A quality-of-life reading also asks whether the person is doing more of what they enjoy, has more control and more relationships, and is less often in situations that lead to distress. Both readings matter. Formal licensing findings belong to DHS Licensing and the processes that govern them, but anyone who touches a person's plan can ask the quality-of-life questions.
lessons.keyPoint: The Positive Supports Rule is about building a good life, not only avoiding forbidden procedures. Restrictive practices are prohibited as a substitute for staffing, as a behavior program, as punishment or for staff convenience.
lessons.example: Tamsin is a DSD program consultant reviewing provider quality data. One provider has had no restraint reports for a year and all paperwork on time. In site visit notes, however, she reads that residents are rarely out in the community, several people spend most evenings in their rooms, and staff describe a 'quiet house' as the goal. Another provider has filed several reports but shows steady growth in outings, jobs and friendships for the people it serves.
lessons.question: What should Tamsin do next?
choices: Treat the first provider as the model because it has no restraint reports.
Treat the second provider as the concern because it files more reports.
Look beyond report counts and ask both providers how they measure and support quality of life, including community participation and choice.
feedback: A clean reporting record is good, but by itself it does not show that people are living full lives. A quiet house can reflect restriction, low staffing or disengagement rather than good support.
More reports can reflect honest reporting and a team that is working actively with someone. Report counts alone cannot tell you whether a provider is doing well or poorly.
This is the strongest response. It uses the rule's own quality-of-life goals as the measure and asks both providers for evidence, without drawing conclusions from counts alone.
lessons.reflection: When you review a provider or a plan, which questions come to you first: compliance questions or quality-of-life questions? What would it take to ask both?
lessons.action: Add two quality-of-life questions, such as how often the person chose an activity this month and how often they were in the community, to the checklist or template you use for your next plan review or site visit.

check.question: Under 245D, restrictive procedures are prohibited when used for which purposes?
check.correct: As a substitute for adequate staffing, as a behavioral or therapeutic program, as punishment, or for staff convenience.
wrong: Only when used as punishment; other uses are allowed with a physician's order.
Only in settings that serve children.
check.feedback: The statute names four purposes: substitute for staffing, behavior program, punishment and staff convenience. Keeping all four in mind helps you spot restrictions that are described in neutral language but serve one of these purposes.

lessons.title: Recognizing prohibited procedures, including subtle ones
objectives: Identify examples of prohibited procedures listed in Minnesota Rules part 9544.0060.
Distinguish subtle deprivation practices from ordinary support.
Explain why removing equipment or requiring people to earn ordinary things is prohibited.
Draft a question to a provider that explores a possible hidden restriction without accusing.
lessons.teaching:
Minnesota Rules part 9544.0060 lists actions and procedures that are prohibited when used as a substitute for adequate staffing, as a behavior program, as punishment or for staff convenience. Some are what most people picture: prone restraint, metal handcuffs or leg hobbles, painful techniques, tripping or pushing, and any action that might restrict a person's airway or breathing. Mechanical and chemical restraint are prohibited, and manual restraint is prohibited except in an emergency under the separate emergency rules.

Many items on the list are subtler and show up in everyday routines. The rule prohibits speaking to a person in a way that ridicules, demeans or threatens; using physical intimidation or a show of force; requiring a person to hold a certain posture; forced exercise; restricting a person's senses; and using intense sounds, lights or noxious sprays. It prohibits isolating or secluding a person without monitoring or when medically contraindicated. It prohibits using one person receiving services to discipline another. It prohibits interfering with a person's legal rights except as the statute allows.

Two items deserve special attention in plan review. First, the rule prohibits denying or restricting access to equipment and devices such as walkers, wheelchairs, hearing aids and communication boards. If temporary removal is needed to prevent injury or serious damage, the device must be returned as soon as the imminent risk has passed. Taking away a communication device is taking away a person's voice. Second, the rule prohibits depriving a person of normal goods and services or requiring them to earn those things, and it prohibits token or level programs that include a response cost or other negative punishment. A plan that says a person earns snacks, phone time or outings by behaving is a warning sign.

Hidden restrictions often come from good intentions, habit or thin staffing. When you see one, ask curious questions first: what is this practice meant to achieve, what happens before the behavior, and what would the person say about it? Formal determinations of whether a violation occurred belong to DHS Licensing and the investigations process. Suspected maltreatment of a vulnerable adult or child must be reported under Minnesota's mandated reporting laws, whatever else is happening.
lessons.keyPoint: Prohibited procedures include subtle practices such as removing a communication device, requiring people to earn ordinary things, or using response cost. Ask curious questions, and report suspected maltreatment through the required channels.
lessons.example: Emeka, a case manager, reads a draft support plan addendum for Lina, who communicates mainly with a tablet. The plan says that when Lina throws objects, staff will put her tablet away for the rest of the day, and that she can earn it back by completing chores. The provider describes this as teaching responsibility. Lina's mother has mentioned that Lina seems withdrawn and has stopped trying to communicate in the evenings.
lessons.question: What should Emeka do next?
choices: Raise the concern with the provider and team: the tablet is a communication device that must be returned once any immediate risk passes, and earning it back is a prohibited practice. Ask what the throwing may be communicating and request a revised plan.
Approve the plan because it does not involve physical restraint.
Suggest the provider keep the rule but shorten it to one hour.
feedback: This is the strongest response. It names the specific concerns under the rule, protects Lina's access to her voice, looks for the function of the behavior and asks for a better plan rather than only rejecting this one.
The rule covers far more than physical restraint. Denying a communication device and requiring a person to earn it back are both listed prohibited practices.
Shortening the time does not solve the problem. The practice still denies Lina her communication device beyond any immediate risk and still makes access conditional on behavior.
lessons.reflection: Think of a routine in a service setting you know that could quietly limit someone's choices. What might it look like from the person's point of view?
lessons.action: In the next support plan or addendum you review, search for words like earn, privilege, lose, removed and until, and ask the team about any practice that makes ordinary goods, activities or equipment conditional on behavior.

check.question: Under Minnesota Rules part 9544.0060, what must happen when a person's walker, hearing aid or communication board is temporarily removed to prevent injury or serious damage?
check.correct: It must be returned as soon as the imminent risk of injury or serious damage has passed.
wrong: It may be withheld until the person completes a behavior plan goal.
It may be withheld for up to twenty-four hours with a supervisor's approval.
check.feedback: The rule allows only temporary removal to prevent injury or serious damage and requires return as soon as that risk passes. Using the device as a reward or holding it for a set period turns it into a prohibited deprivation.

lessons.title: Emergency use of manual restraint and reporting
objectives: Explain the two conditions that must both be met for emergency use of manual restraint under 245D.
Describe the reporting and review sequence that follows an emergency use.
Identify events that providers must report on the behavior intervention report form.
Plan how oversight staff can use reports to improve a person's supports.
lessons.teaching:
Minnesota Statutes section 245D.061 allows emergency use of manual restraint only when two conditions are both met: immediate intervention is needed to protect the person or others from imminent risk of physical harm, and the type of manual restraint is the least restrictive intervention that will eliminate the immediate risk and achieve safety. The restraint must end when the threat of harm ends. Staff must monitor the person's health and welfare during the restraint, and when possible the monitoring staff member should be someone other than the person implementing it. Providers must have a written policy, and staff must be trained before they may use emergency manual restraint. A provider may also choose not to allow it and must then describe the alternatives staff will use.

The statute sets a review sequence. Within three calendar days, the staff member who implemented the restraint reports in writing to the designated coordinator, including what less restrictive steps were tried, for how long, the person's condition before and after, any injuries and whether a debriefing happened. Within five working days of the restraint, the provider completes an internal review asking whether the person's supports need to change, whether policies were followed and adequate, and whether training or corrective action is needed. Within five working days after that, the provider consults the expanded support team to identify what led to the behavior, what function it may have served and whether the plan should change. Within five working days of that review, the provider sends the report, internal review and team summary to DHS and the Office of the Ombudsman for Mental Health and Developmental Disabilities.

The Positive Supports Rule also requires providers to use the DHS behavior intervention report form for several events, including any emergency use of manual restraint, a medical emergency or mental health crisis caused by a restrictive intervention, a behavioral incident that leads to a 911 call, an incident requiring a call to mobile crisis services, and use of an as-needed medication to intervene in a behavioral situation. Under part 9544.0070, three emergency uses of manual restraint within ninety days, or four within one hundred eighty days, trigger a positive support transition plan.

For case managers and oversight staff, these reports are information about a person's life. A cluster of reports often means something in the environment, staffing, health or plan is not working. Read them looking for patterns, and ask what will change.
lessons.keyPoint: Emergency manual restraint is allowed only for imminent risk of physical harm, only in the least restrictive form and only until the threat ends. Each use triggers written reports and reviews, and repeated use triggers a positive support transition plan.
lessons.example: Priya is a county case manager for Deshawn, who lives in a 245D licensed home. Over six weeks she receives three behavior intervention reports describing emergency manual restraint during evening shift changes. Each report lists slightly different staff, and the internal reviews say policies were followed. No one has mentioned a positive support transition plan, and Deshawn has told Priya he hates it when new staff come in without saying who they are.
lessons.question: What should Priya do next?
choices: File the reports because the provider says policies were followed.

Ask the provider whether a positive support transition plan is now required, share the pattern she sees at shift changes and what Deshawn has told her, and request an expanded support team meeting that includes him.
Ask the provider to stop reporting unless an injury occurs, to reduce paperwork.
feedback: Policies being followed does not mean supports are working. Three emergency restraints within ninety days meets the threshold for a positive support transition plan, and the pattern needs attention.
This is the strongest response. It applies the ninety-day threshold, brings a likely cause into view, adds Deshawn's own words and uses the team process the statute requires.
Reporting is required for every emergency use of manual restraint, not only when someone is hurt. Suggesting less reporting would undermine the safeguards the law puts in place.
lessons.reflection: When a report arrives in your queue, what do you usually do with it? What would it look like to read it as a message about someone's day?
lessons.action: Pull the last three months of behavior intervention reports for one person you serve or oversee, and note the time of day, setting and staffing pattern for each event.

check.question: Under Minnesota Rules part 9544.0070, when must a license holder develop a positive support transition plan?
check.correct: After three incidents of emergency use of manual restraint within ninety days or four within one hundred eighty days.
wrong: After any single emergency use of manual restraint.
Only when a person is injured during a restraint.
check.feedback: The rule sets a frequency threshold: three within ninety days or four within one hundred eighty days. Every single emergency use still requires reports and reviews under 245D.061, and injury is not the trigger.

lessons.title: Transition plans and person-centered positive behavior support
objectives: Describe the timelines for a positive support transition plan under 245D.
Explain how functional behavior assessment and positive behavior support shape a good plan.
Identify the role of the External Program Review Committee.
Plan quality-of-life measures to track alongside behavior data.
lessons.teaching:
A positive support transition plan is the tool 245D uses to phase out restrictive practices safely. License holders must develop one, on DHS forms, for a person who requires intervention to maintain safety when it is known the person's behavior poses an immediate risk of physical harm to self or others. For people admitted after the transition to the current rules, the plan must be developed and put in place within thirty calendar days of starting services and must phase out prohibited interventions no later than eleven months from when the plan starts. DHS notes that some providers need more time to phase out a procedure therapeutically and has a process for requesting approval.

The External Program Review Committee, set up under part 9544.0130, includes an expert in positive supports, a mental health professional, a licensed health professional and a representative of the Department of Health. It monitors how the rule is implemented, reviews requests for emergency use of procedures and requests to temporarily use a prohibited procedure, reviews emergency manual restraint reports and gives guidance to license holders. DHS will not grant a permanent variance to allow a prohibited procedure.

The content of a plan matters as much as the timeline. The rule calls for person-centered planning and functional behavior assessment, which asks what happens before a behavior, what the person gets or avoids through it, and what else is going on in their life. Positive Supports Minnesota describes positive behavior support as research-based work that improves quality of life and reduces challenging behavior by changing social interactions and settings, teaching communication and social skills, and staying person-centered and culturally responsive. A good plan changes the environment and the support around the person and teaches new ways to meet the same need. It does not only describe what staff will do when things go wrong.

Quality of life is the real measure. Alongside counts of incidents, track things the person cares about: time spent in activities they chose, relationships, sleep, health, work or school, and how often they say no and are listened to. A plan that reduces incidents while shrinking a person's life has not succeeded.
lessons.keyPoint: A positive support transition plan must be in place within thirty days and phase out prohibited procedures within eleven months. Good plans rest on functional assessment and positive behavior support and are judged by quality of life, not only incident counts.
lessons.example: Bao, a DSD policy analyst, is helping a lead agency review transition plans. One plan for Yusuf includes detailed data on incidents and a clear list of staff responses, but says nothing about what Yusuf likes, what the behavior may be communicating, or what skills he will learn. The plan is on track to meet the eleven-month timeline. The team asks Bao whether the plan is acceptable because it meets every deadline.
lessons.question: What should Bao advise?
choices: Approve the plan because it meets the timeline and the data are thorough.
Recommend adding restrictions to guarantee the incident count keeps falling.

Say the timeline is only part of the picture, and recommend adding a functional behavior assessment summary, strategies that teach Yusuf new ways to meet his needs, and quality-of-life measures he helps choose.
feedback: Meeting deadlines is necessary but not enough. Without an understanding of what the behavior is for and a plan to build skills and improve Yusuf's life, restrictions may simply return later.
Adding restrictions runs directly against the purpose of the plan, which is to phase restrictive practices out, and it risks introducing prohibited procedures.
This is the strongest response. It keeps the timeline, adds the person-centered and functional elements the rule expects and measures success by Yusuf's quality of life.
lessons.reflection: What would you want a support team to track if they were measuring whether your own life was going well?
lessons.action: Choose one plan you work with and write down two quality-of-life measures the person would care about. Suggest them to the team at the next review.

check.question: What does functional behavior assessment mainly try to understand?
check.correct: What happens before a behavior and what purpose the behavior serves for the person, so supports can meet that need in a better way.
wrong: Which restrictive procedure will stop the behavior fastest.
Whether the person's diagnosis explains the behavior so no changes are needed.
check.feedback: Functional behavior assessment looks for the triggers and purpose of a behavior. That understanding lets a team change the environment and teach new skills, which is the heart of positive behavior support. It is not a way to choose a restriction or to excuse the behavior with a diagnosis.

cards.back: Minnesota Rules chapter 9544, governing positive support strategies and restrictive interventions in 245D services and certain 245A licensed settings for people with developmental disabilities or related conditions.
Restrictive procedures may not be used as a substitute for adequate staffing, as a behavior program, as punishment or for staff convenience.
Allowed only when needed to protect someone from imminent risk of physical harm, in the least restrictive form, and ending when the threat ends. Each use triggers written reports and reviews.
A DHS-form plan to phase out restrictive interventions, developed within thirty calendar days of service start and phased out within eleven months.
An assessment of what happens before a behavior and what purpose it serves, used to design positive supports.

aid.heading: Plan review: look for hidden restrictions
items: Words like earn, lose, privilege, removed or until attached to ordinary goods, activities or equipment.
Removal of communication devices, mobility aids or hearing aids beyond immediate risk.
Token or level systems that take away points or privileges.
Isolation, seclusion or time alone without monitoring.
Any practice that could be a substitute for staffing, a behavior program, punishment or staff convenience.

aid.heading: After an emergency manual restraint
items: Written staff report to the designated coordinator within three calendar days.
Provider internal review within five working days.
Expanded support team review within five working days after the internal review.
Submission to DHS and the Ombudsman for Mental Health and Developmental Disabilities within five working days after the team review.
Positive support transition plan if there are three uses in ninety days or four in one hundred eighty days.

aid.heading: Quality of life check
items: How often did the person choose their own activities this month?
How much time did they spend in the community and with people they like?
What new skills are they learning to meet the needs behind the behavior?
When they said no, were they listened to?

aid.heading: Route it correctly
items: Suspected maltreatment: report through Minnesota's mandated reporting channels right away.
Requests for temporary use of a prohibited procedure or variances: DHS, with External Program Review Committee review.
Plan content and supports: the person and their expanded support team.
